comment: Every status claim in README.md's Features table resolves to an entry here.
`scripts/readme-status-gate.js` parses that table and fails when a status cell is not a vocabulary word
allowed here, when the word is stronger than the evidence recorded against the feature, or when a feature
The vocabulary is deliberately weak. `tested` says a test exists that exercises the feature; it does not say
the feature is correct. `verified` is reserved for a claim backed by an artifact this project produced and
can be pointed at — and it is withheld where an audit has found the opposite.
Rules learned the hard way in this repository: a benchmark figure without a citation, and an install command
that returns 404, both shipped for months because nothing checked the text against the evidence.

MCP Server.note: The code has 48 `registry.register(...)` calls and 46 distinct names, computed by scripts/doc-code-sync-gate.js. The README previously said 45 and had done so since before the audit; it now states the computed figure. The gap between 48 calls and 46 names is unresolved — it is either two duplicate registrations or two names the parser does not read, and the entry stays `partial` until that is settled.

VS Code Extension.evidence: packages/vscode — 780 tests, run separately in CI

Web Dashboard.note: packages/web is excluded from the root coverage run and has its own configuration; the tests exist but are not part of the measured body.

Impact Analysis.note: Five defects in this path were fixed on 2026-09-17 (0a6418d, e505ea2, b7337e1, 2b80922, 3ec10ee). Before that date the feature ran on fallbacks and this row's claim would have been false.

Cross-Repo Analysis.evidence: benchmarks/cross-repo-matrix.json, produced by .github/workflows/cross-repo-real.yml from flask 3.0.3 + werkzeug 3.0.3 in one workspace: 49 of 49 import pairs resolved (recall 1.0, precision 1.0, imported names 1.0), trace 73/73, impact 49/49, every expected answer from Python's own ast. Acceptance suite: tests/e2e/cross-repo-real-workspace.test.ts (5 cases on the two checkouts).
Cross-Repo Analysis.note: Until this measurement the story's evidence was a fixture: both repositories were temporary directories linked with `../../`, and the real pair - two packages released separately, linked by name - produced 0 import edges. The five defects that made the fixture pass are fixed; the package-name resolver is what makes the claim true for a released dependency.

Taint Analysis.evidence: benchmarks/owasp-benchmark.json, produced by .github/workflows/owasp-benchmark.yml from OWASP-Benchmark/BenchmarkJava at commit f40c618: 2740 labelled cases, 1415 real vulnerabilities, TPR 0.8170, FPR 0.3042, score 0.5128. The engine is scored in two halves over the same corpus: the flow analysis alone scores 0.1510 (TPR 0.4551, FPR 0.3042) and the rule family alone 0.3625 (TPR 0.3625, FPR 0). Over the seven flow categories the flow analysis scores 0.2066 (TPR 0.7129, FPR 0.5063). Acceptance suite: tests/e2e/owasp-benchmark.test.ts (7 cases: a named vulnerable case, a named escaped one, a named file write that must not read as cross-site scripting, named cases for three of the four rule categories, and a repeat-run determinism check).
Taint Analysis.note: The four categories a flow cannot answer now have a rule family of their own, and they are why the score moved 0.1695 -> 0.4479: 513 of 513 vulnerable cases found across crypto, hash, weakrand and securecookie, at a false-positive rate of 0. Two of the rules read the project's own configuration, because the corpus selects its algorithm with `benchmark.properties` (`hashAlg1=MD5`) rather than at the call. **A `write` is not one sink**: the vocabulary matched a method name, and a method name names no destination, so 85 safe `Crypto` cases were charged for writing ciphertext into a file whose path was fixed when the writer was constructed. Filtering `html` sinks by the receiver's declared type moved the score 0.4479 -> 0.5128 and left crypto, hash, weakrand and securecookie all at TPR 1.000 with FPR 0. The remaining defect is precision in the flow half: FPR 0.3042 costs more than every miss combined, and the measured causes are a single-block CFG with no path sensitivity (151 of the 403 false positives contain the corpus's constant-condition dead branch) and statement-level neutralisation.

Benchmark Framework.note: The suite holds 49 ground-truth issues, below the 100 this project requires before publishing a figure, and the README now says no figures are published. The framework runs, so `partial` rather than absent — but `Verified — benchmark tested` contradicted the section directly above it.

Knowledge Graph.evidence: packages/shared/src/types/graph.ts declares NODE_LABELS (36) and RELATIONSHIP_TYPES (43); counted on 2026-09-17 and matching the README

19-Phase Analysis Pipeline.note: The phase count is not verified against the pipeline, and no single test exercises the pipeline end to end. Recorded as partial rather than asserted.

31-Language Parsing.note: The language count is asserted and not counted here. The 2026-08-17 audit notes the language parsers were excluded from coverage, so their tests were not part of the measured body.

Security Rule Families.evidence: benchmarks/owasp-benchmark.json > byEngine.rules: TPR 0.3625, FPR 0.0000, score 0.3625 over all 2740 cases; within the four categories the rules answer, 513 of 513 vulnerable and 0 of 529 safe. Acceptance suites: tests/e2e/owasp-benchmark.test.ts (two cases over the real corpus) and packages/intelligence/src/__tests__/security-rule-families.test.ts (30 cases, 99% statements and 98% branches). Gate: scripts/owasp-benchmark-gate.js holds every category at TPR 1.0 and the rule family's own FPR at 0.
Security Rule Families.note: Four rules for Java: weak-cipher, weak-hash, weak-random, insecure-cookie. They are a rule family rather than a flow because the bug is a property of a call — 'this program chose DES' — and no path analysis reaches it. `evaluateSecurityRules` takes configuration as an input, which is what makes it the first capability here that needs the index rather than one file: 258 of the corpus's hash and crypto cases name their algorithm through `getProperty`, and the answer is in `benchmark.properties`. Only Java is covered; `ruleCoverage()` reports that rather than letting an empty result read as clean.
